Answer. The claimed win does not hold for building a course from nothing (measured). With the CLI, the agent used more tokens, more round trips and more checker runs, and produced courses the judges scored lower. On revising, the CLI leans cheaper and is just as reliable, but 5 runs per arm are too few to show it. Rendering gaps in lessons.mjs explain most of the quality loss, and both look fixable (inferred from the judges' reasons and the page counts).

RECOMMENDATION:
1. Fix the three rendering gaps before relying on the CLI for new courses. Make the inline-code tail lazy, either support or reject multi-line «…», and have check reject leftover backticks, markers and double escapes in rendered text. Add a test with a one-character span. This is the cause of most of the quality loss (inferred), and it is a small change in one file.
  2. Then rerun the build arm only. 5 CLI builds against the 5 old-flow builds already graded, about 22 list dollars. If quality reaches parity, the CLI's remaining build cost is turns, not defects.
  3. Cut build turns. The CLI flow writes one lesson per call and checks once per unit, so it takes about 1.7× the turns, and each turn re-reads the whole context. Writing a whole unit in one call and checking once per unit should close part of the gap (guess). It would need a measured rerun.
  4. Keep the CLI for revisions. It is at least as reliable and leans cheaper, and the folder of lesson files keeps an edit local to one lesson. It also enforces phone-width code, which the old flow shipped broken in every build.
DESIGN:
• Without CLI. The skill at commit c4f17c3. The agent copies template.html, writes the COURSE, UNITS and GLOSSARY block by hand, keeps syllabus.md in step, and runs check.mjs.
  • With CLI. The skill at 566c86e on main. The agent writes course.json, syllabus.md and one markdown file per lesson, then runs lessons.mjs check and build.
  • Subject. The ky HTTP client at commit 3541888, 3 to 4 units, the same for every run.
  • Same everything else. claude-opus-5-5 at high effort, headless claude -p, the same byte-identical prompt. The skill sits at the same path in each workspace and only its contents differ. The user-level install of the skill was blocked, and transcripts confirm that no run read outside its own workspace and session folders.
  • Revise seed. One finished CLI build with two planted defects: a fill card with two blanks in lesson u4l1, and a code line joined to 54 columns in u1l1. The old arm got the same content as a c4f17c3 page.
  • Runs. 5 per arm per task, 20 in all, 5 at a time with the arms interleaved. Five is the smallest count where a complete separation reaches p below 0.01. It can show a large effect and will miss a small one.
  • Grading. The current check.mjs grades every final page. A script checks the three revise requests. Two blind judges, one Opus and one Sonnet, scored markdown dumps under shuffled letters against a rubric written before any run.

The plan, rubric, prompts and harness are in evals/lessons-cli/ on the eval-lessons-cli branch.
BUG:
Measured
The inline-code pattern in scripts/lessons.mjs (line 70) has a greedy optional tail. A one-character span such as `/` or `?` pairs with the next backtick on the line instead of its own. The spans after it turn inside out, so prose renders as code and code as prose.

In the source, That makes `'sort=new&limit=5'` and `'?sort=new&limit=5'` send the same query. rendered on the page as That makes </code>'sort=new&limit=5'<code>and</code>….

Four of five CLI builds shipped 3 to 6 such strings (measured). Three of five CLI revisions added 1 or 2 more in the lesson they inserted (measured). lessons.mjs check passes every one of these pages, so neither agent nor user is told. Four revise runs noticed the garbled text in the seed's u2l1 and fixed it by hand, which is most of the "collateral" edits in the revise table (measured from the diffs). The fix is likely to make the tail lazy, (?:[^\n]*?[^`\n])??, plus a test with a one-character span (inferred, untested).

Two more rendering gaps

  • Multi-line highlights leak. mark in scripts/lessons.mjs (line 26) applies «…» only within one line. Agents wrap long highlighted lines to meet the 41-column rule, and the raw markers then reach the page: 4 strings in one CLI build and 1 in another (measured). references/lessons.md does not say a highlight must stay on one line.
  • Entities inside code spans are escaped twice. An agent wrote `.json<User>()` inside a raw HTML paragraph. The CLI escaped it again, and the learner sees <User> (measured, one course).

The checker passes all three defects. A check that rejects a backtick inside rendered <code>, a leftover « or », or &lt; in course text would have caught every case in this eval (inferred from the counts above).
LIMITS_GENERAL:
• Sample size. 5 runs per arm. A complete separation gives p = 0.008. A real 20% difference would usually not reach p below 0.05 here, so "no clear difference" means "not shown", not "equal".
  • Input tokens are cache reads. About 97% of input tokens in every run are cache reads, and their count grows with turns times context size. A flow with more, smaller turns costs more here even when it reads and writes less. Cache writes and output tokens are closer to the work itself.
  • The width rule is new. Only the CLI's checker enforces 41-column code lines. Old-arm builds shipped 34 to 86 wide lines unflagged. That makes the CLI look worse on checker failures and better on final pass rate for the same reason. The table shows both rows.
  • The seed came from the CLI arm. Its lesson text was written in the CLI's markdown format and carries the garbled-span bug. The old arm got the same content as JSON in a c4f17c3 page, which is tidier than a hand-written block. This favours neither arm in an obvious way, but it is not a seed the old flow made.
  • Browser click-through. The prompts say the user will click through the course themselves. Many runs opened a browser anyway (0 to 42 calls), which adds tool calls and turns unevenly.
  • Shared environment. Runs kept the user's settings and hooks, the same for both arms. Other apps loaded the machine during the runs. Wall time is the noisiest number here.
  • Judges. One pass per judge model, scoring text dumps rather than the rendered page. Figures appear only as a placeholder naming their element count. The dump glues flow-diagram labels together, and one judge counted that against craft. The two judges agree only loosely on single courses, so read the arm means, not single scores.
  • Prior evidence. An earlier real 19-unit build on another codebase with the old flow ran the checker 34 times with 4 failures, wrote helper scripts, and spent about 69 calls in 5 subagents rewrapping wide lines. Course size and setup differ from this eval, so it only shows which old-flow costs the CLI targets.
COST: In runs, the eval used 20 candidate runs and 2 judge runs, with no reruns and no rate-limit stops. Build runs averaged about 3.96 list dollars each and revise runs about 1.88. The planned pause point was 40 per build, and no run came near it. The CLI does not report what share of the subscription's usage limit this took, so that share is not measured here.
